title: Soil Testing: Why and How
summary: Regular soil testing helps you understand what nutrients your land has and what it lacks. This prevents over-use of fertilisers and saves money.
key_points: Test soil once every 2 years minimum
Collect samples from multiple spots in the field
Test for pH, nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and micronutrients
Use results to apply the right fertilisers in the right amounts
Soil Health Card scheme provides free testing through government
disclaimer: Recommendations based on soil tests are advisory. Consult a local agronomist for specific guidance.

title: Drip Irrigation: Water-Saving Approach
summary: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone, reducing water use by up to 50% compared to flood irrigation while maintaining or improving crop yield.
key_points: Suitable for vegetables, fruits, sugarcane, cotton, and orchard crops
Reduces water consumption significantly
Reduces weed growth as only root zone is wetted
Drip fertigation allows nutrients to be applied with water
Government subsidy available through PMKSY (Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana)
disclaimer: Drip system design should be done by a qualified agronomist or irrigation engineer for your specific field.

title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Basics
summary: IPM is a sustainable approach to managing pests by combining biological, cultural, and chemical methods to minimise economic, health, and environmental risks.
key_points: Scout fields regularly to identify pests before they cause major damage
Use resistant crop varieties where available
Biological control: encourage natural predators like ladybirds and spiders
Cultural practices: crop rotation, proper spacing, timely sowing
Use chemical pesticides only as a last resort, follow label instructions strictly
Never mix pesticides unless specifically recommended
source: ICAR / Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine & Storage
disclaimer: Pesticide application should follow label instructions. Consult Krishi Vigyan Kendra for identification of specific pests and diseases.

title: Post-Harvest Handling to Reduce Losses
summary: Approximately 20-30% of fresh produce is lost post-harvest in India due to improper handling, storage, and transportation. Simple practices can significantly reduce these losses.
key_points: Harvest at proper maturity — not too early, not too late
Handle produce gently to prevent bruising
Clean and sort produce before storage
Pre-cool vegetables and fruits if possible before transport
Use clean, ventilated containers for transport
Store in cool, dry, clean conditions
Do not store near chemicals or pesticides
disclaimer: Specific handling requirements vary by crop. Consult APMC or Krishi Vigyan Kendra for crop-specific advice.

title: Crop Rotation for Soil Health
summary: Growing different crops in sequence on the same field improves soil health, reduces pest buildup, and can reduce fertiliser needs.
key_points: Alternate between legume crops (dal, groundnut) and cereals
Legumes fix nitrogen in soil, reducing need for nitrogen fertiliser
Breaks pest and disease cycles that target specific crops
Improves soil structure over time
Plan rotations based on local climate and market demand
source: ICAR / Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare
disclaimer: Optimal rotation depends on your local soil, climate, and available irrigation. Seek local agronomist advice.

title: Preparing Your Produce for Market
summary: How you present your produce at the mandi affects the price you receive. Grading, cleaning, and proper packaging improve market price significantly.
key_points: Sort and grade produce by size, color, and quality before taking to market
Remove damaged, rotted, or off-spec produce to avoid dragging down average grade
Clean produce (remove soil, leaves) — cleaner lots fetch higher prices
Use standardised bags/boxes where possible
Know the current mandi price before you go — do not accept first quote blindly
e-NAM registration allows you to get competitive bids from multiple buyers
source: NAFED / National Horticulture Board / Ministry of Agriculture
disclaimer: Market prices vary by day, mandi, and quality. Verify prices through KisanLink or direct mandi inquiry.

title: On-Farm Storage Basics
summary: Proper storage allows farmers to wait for better market prices and avoid distress selling immediately after harvest when prices are typically lowest.
key_points: Store grains at less than 12-14% moisture content to prevent fungal growth
Use hermetic (airtight) storage bags to reduce pest damage in grains
Keep storage area clean, dry, and pest-free
Warehouse receipts from registered warehouses allow loans against stored produce
Check Negotiable Warehouse Receipt (NWR) scheme at WDRA (wdra.gov.in)
Never store near pesticides or chemicals
source: Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (WDRA) / Ministry of Agriculture
disclaimer: Storage conditions vary by crop. For large volumes, consult a cold chain or warehouse specialist.

title: Introduction to Organic Farming
summary: Organic farming relies on natural inputs and avoids synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. It can fetch premium prices but requires certification for market claims.
key_points: Uses compost, vermicompost, and natural manures instead of synthetic fertilisers
Uses biological pest control and crop rotation instead of synthetic pesticides
Certification required to sell as 'organic' — contact APEDA or state agriculture dept
Transition period: 2-3 years from conventional to certified organic
PGS-India (Participatory Guarantee System) is a simpler certification for small farmers
Check APEDA for organic export opportunities
disclaimer: Organic certification requirements are specific and legally binding. Do not claim 'organic' without proper certification.
